headline: Tiny Bolivian wild cat turns out to be a new species

sources.title: Tiny wild cat newly identified as a species draws curious visitors in Bolivia (AP)
Meet the Adorable and Tiny Tilcayo, the First Brand-New Cat Species Identified in More Than a Century (Smithsonian Magazine)
Meet the First New Cat Species Discovered in 100 Years (National Geographic)

chunks.text: A tiny wild cat from Bolivia's [[cloud forests]] has {{turned out to be}} a new species. It lives on the eastern slopes of the Andes Mountains. Scientists say it is the first new wild cat species [[described]] in more than a century. A study about the cat {{came out}} in the [[journal]] Current Biology on September 17, 2026.

verbs.correct: To be discovered to be something
verbs.wrong: To slowly change into a different thing
verbs.why: The quiet new neighbor turned out to be a famous singer. The old painting in the attic turned out to be very valuable. The small spotted cat that a family once kept as a pet has turned out to be a species new to science.

verbs.correct: To be published for the public
verbs.wrong: To be checked by other experts
verbs.why: Her first novel came out last spring. A new report on city traffic comes out every January. The study describing the new cat species came out in the journal Current Biology on September 17, 2026.

chunks.text: One of these cats, a male, lives at a [[wildlife sanctuary]] near La Paz. A local family {{took in}} the cat as a [[kitten]] and tried to raise him as a [[house cat]]. In 2017, they brought him to the sanctuary. Researchers later {{carried out}} a [[genetic study]] comparing the full [[genomes]] of 38 related wild cats. It showed that the new species {{branched off}} from its closest [[relatives]] about 1.4 million years ago.

verbs.correct: To give a person or animal a home
verbs.wrong: To hire someone to work for you
verbs.why: My aunt took in a stray dog she found in the rain. The couple took in two foster children last year. A local family took in the cat as a kitten and tried to raise him as a house cat.

verbs.correct: To do a planned piece of research
verbs.wrong: To keep doing the same task
verbs.why: The school carried out a survey of its students. Engineers will carry out safety tests on the bridge next week. Researchers carried out a genetic study that compared the full genomes of 38 related wild cats.

verbs.correct: To separate from a main line or group
verbs.wrong: To start doing new kinds of things
verbs.why: A narrow path branches off from the main trail near the lake. Spanish and Italian branched off from Latin many centuries ago. The genetic study showed that the new species branched off from its closest relatives about 1.4 million years ago.

chunks.text: The male cat weighs about 3 pounds and is smaller than the average house cat. His unusually large spots {{stand out}} on his light brown fur. The study {{set off}} a [[wave of excitement]] on social media. Since then, visitors from across Bolivia and beyond have {{shown up}} at the sanctuary. But the cat is [[easily stressed]] by people. [[Caretakers]] keep him out of [[public view]] and {{turn away}} crowds hoping for a closer look.

verbs.correct: To be very easy to notice
verbs.why: A yellow car stands out in a busy parking lot. Her bright red coat stood out in the crowd. The little cat's unusually large spots stand out on his light brown fur.
One angry post can set off a long online fight. The late goal set off a huge celebration in the stadium. The study set off a wave of excitement about the tiny cat on social media.
Only ten people showed up for the meeting. Fans showed up at the airport hours before the band landed. Visitors from across Bolivia and beyond have shown up at the sanctuary hoping to see the cat.

verbs.correct: To refuse to let people enter
verbs.wrong: To hand something to an official
verbs.why: The concert was full, so the staff turned away hundreds of fans. The hotel had no free rooms and turned away late guests. The cat is easily stressed by people, so caretakers turn away crowds hoping for a closer look.

chunks.text: The sanctuary's co-founder said the cat became "an [[ambassador]] for conservation" in just a few days. He said the news has helped [[raise awareness]] about protecting wild cats and their forest [[habitat]]. Threats to the cats include [[deforestation]] and [[wildlife trafficking]]. The study also {{sorted out}} the [[family tree]] of the cat's group, the tiger cats. The group now has five species. A wild cat expert {{pointed out}} that this means fewer animals in each species.

verbs.correct: To bring order to something confusing
verbs.wrong: To look through things one at a time
verbs.why: A new manager sorted out the messy work schedule in a week. Our teacher sorted out the confusion about the test dates. The study sorted out the family tree of the tiger cats, a group that now has five species.

verbs.correct: To mention a fact people should notice
verbs.wrong: To be a sign that something is true
verbs.why: My friend pointed out a mistake in my email. The guide pointed out that the museum closes early on Sundays. A wild cat expert pointed out that with five species, each one has fewer animals.

mainIdea.s: A small cat kept at a Bolivian sanctuary has been confirmed as a species new to science. The news has brought crowds to the sanctuary and more attention to wild cats and their forests.
mainIdea.why: Genetic tests showed the cat is a separate species. The sanctuary's co-founder says it became an ambassador for conservation in just a few days.

mainIdea.s: Scientists have confirmed that a little spotted cat from Bolivia is a separate species. Its caretakers now show it to large crowds each day to raise money for forest protection.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the cat is easily stressed by people. Caretakers keep him out of public view and turn the crowds away.

mainIdea.s: Rangers in the mountains of Bolivia filmed a rare spotted wild cat for the first time in decades. They believe a small group still survives there despite years of forest loss.
mainIdea.why: No rare cat was filmed in the mountains. A cat living at a sanctuary near La Paz was identified as a new species through genetic tests.

lines.text: Did you hear about the tiny wild cat in Bolivia? It {{turned out to be}} a brand-new species.
A new cat species? I thought we knew every kind of cat by now.
Scientists say it's the first new wild cat species identified in more than a century. The study {{came out}} on September 17.
At a wildlife sanctuary near La Paz. A local family {{took him in}} as a kitten and tried to raise him as a house cat.
So a new species was [[hiding in plain sight]] in somebody's living room.
For about a year, yes. Later, researchers {{carried out}} a genetic study. It showed his species {{branched off}} from its relatives about 1.4 million years ago.
He weighs about three pounds, so he's smaller than a house cat. And his big spots really {{stand out}}.
I bet everyone wants to see him.
They do. The news {{set off}} a lot of excitement online, and visitors keep {{showing up}} at the sanctuary.
Poor guy, suddenly [[in the spotlight]]. Do they get to see him?
Not really. He gets stressed around people, so the caretakers {{turn away}} the crowds.
The sanctuary's co-founder calls him an ambassador for conservation now. He's helping people care about wild cats and their forests.
[[Small but mighty]]. Did the study find anything else?
It {{sorted out}} the family tree of tiger cats. There are five species now, and one expert {{pointed out}} that this leaves fewer animals in each one.
So this little cat is putting those forests [[on the map]].
